Situation1: Include each other in social activities and outings when possible.
Expectation2: Support individuals or groups in accessing essential services and resources
Situation2: They casually guide a youth, an older adult, or a refugee family toward available social or community services.
Story: I stared at my phone, torn between two text threads. My younger brother had just messaged, asking if I could join him and his friends for dinner. He’d been trying to include me more, hoping we could rebuild the closeness we’d lost over the years. I knew how much it meant to him—he wanted us to be more than just siblings who passed each other in the hallway. At the same time, a refugee family I’d been working with sent a message, asking if I could help them navigate the community center’s registration process that evening. As their advocate, I was often their only link to resources they desperately needed. I felt the weight of both expectations pressing down on me: my brother’s hope for a stronger bond, and the family’s trust in my support. My mind raced, guilt and anxiety swirling as I tried to figure out how to be present for both. I wanted to be a good brother, but I also couldn’t let down those who depended on me. My thumb hovered over the screen, paralyzed by the impossible choice.
